title: Jesus of Nazareth
lead: Jesus of Nazareth, a Jewish teacher and healer from Galilee, crucified by the Roman governor Pontius Pilate around AD 30, whom his followers proclaimed as the Messiah, the Son of God, raised from the dead. The four Gospels tell his story; the rest of the New Testament explains what it means. The New Testament presents him as the fulfillment of Israel's hopes for a coming king, prophet and servant (see messiah).

sections.b: Iēsous is the Greek form of the Hebrew Yehoshua or Yeshua, "the LORD saves," the same name as Joshua son of Nun. It was one of the most common Jewish names of the time; Josephus mentions more than a dozen men called Jesus. Matthew draws out the meaning: "he is the one who will save his people from their sins" (Matthew 1:21). "Christ" is not a surname but the Greek for Messiah, "anointed one" (see the topic messiah).

Almost all historians, Christian, Jewish and secular, agree that Jesus was a real Jew from Nazareth in Galilee, that he was baptized by John the Baptist, that he gathered disciples and taught about the kingdom of God, that he had a reputation as a healer and exorcist, that he caused a disturbance at the Temple, and that he was crucified under Pontius Pilate (governor AD 26–36). Roman and Jewish writers mention him: Josephus (Jewish Antiquities 18.63–64, a passage later expanded by Christian copyists, and 20.200, on "James, the brother of Jesus who was called Christ") and Tacitus (Annals 15.44). Beyond this core, historians weigh each saying and story differently (E. P. Sanders, John P. Meier, Geza Vermes, Paula Fredriksen, N. T. Wright).

Matthew, Mark and Luke (the "Synoptic" Gospels, which can be "seen together") tell much the same story in much the same order, often in the same words; John tells it differently. How the first three are related is the Synoptic problem (see that topic). Each Gospel paints its own portrait: Matthew's Jesus is the son of David and the new Moses who teaches with authority, Mark's the Son of God who serves and suffers, Luke's the Savior of the poor and the outsider, John's the Word made flesh.
